KEY MESSAGE 1: Cool weather will linger into the weekend. Near 
to slightly above normal temperatures return next week.

GOES-E visible imagery and 25/17z surface analysis showed the 
deepening Nor'easter well to the northeast of Cape Hatteras with
1026 hPa high pressure centered over Lake Superior extending 
into the Southeast U.S. and Deep South. Direct influences from 
the departing Nor'easter will gradually wane this afternoon with
gusty north/northwest winds quickly diminishing as sunset 
approaches. Tonight looks to favor a solid radiational night. 
The boundary layer should decouple fairly quickly this evening 
and with fairly low dewpoints in place, temperatures should 
steadily fall under clear skies. Typical for radiational nights,
the 25/13z NBM looks to exhibit a warm bias through daybreak
Sunday which is best highlighted by the large interquartile 
range (as much as 4-7 degrees) at various observation sites 
across the Lowcountry and Southeast Georgia. The coldest of the 
guidance was favored for lows tonight as a result, ranging from
the upper 40s/lower 50s inland to the lower 60s at the beaches,
with further local adjustments made to account for typical and 
well know mesoscale influences (i.e. Charleston Harbor, Broad 
River, Santee-Cooper lakes, Francis Marion National Forest, 
etc).

Temperatures will begin to moderate Saturday as ridging builds
aloft and surface high pressure maintains its influence on the
region. Highs look to warm into the upper 70s/lower 80s and are
fairly consistent with full-sun 850-1000 hPa thickness schemes.
Saturday night into Sunday morning will likely be another cool 
night with strong radiational cooling likely coming into play 
again within a decoupled boundary layer. The lower side of the 
guidance envelop was favored with lows ranging from the lower 
50s well inland to the lower-mid 60s at the beaches.

Dry conditions look to persist into much of next week with 
broad high pressure prevailing. Temperatures will continue to
moderate with near to slightly above average conditions
expected. The next chances for rainfall should hold off until
Thursday into Friday of next week as net moisture values begin
to build back into the area along the backside of subtropical 
high pressure centered well offshore over the Atlantic.


KEY MESSAGE 2: The coastal flood risk will linger into early
next week.

As a nor'easter churns offshore of the Mid-Atlantic coastline, 
breezy north-northeasterly flow will continue across the region.
The combination of breezy winds with the full moon today will 
result in minor (possibly moderate) coastal flooding with each 
high tide cycle through the weekend (esp. for the Charleston 
Harbor).

Charleston Harbor: With the ongoing environmental conditions, 
tidal levels could reach 7.4 ft MLLW in the Charleston Harbor 
for this evening's high tide (approx. at 755PM). Therefore, 
Coastal Flood Advisory has been issued from 6PM to 10PM this 
evening for Charleston and Colleton Counties. Saltwater 
inundation will be possible 2 to 3 hours before and after high 
tide, and will likely result in some roads becoming impassable.

Coastal flooding concerns will continue tomorrow (9/26) with 
the potential to reach moderate flood stage for Charleston and 
Colleton County with the morning high tide (~8AM). Thereafter, 
it's likely to see minor coastal flooding conditions through 
early next week for the Charleston Harbor.

Fort Pulaski: Tidal levels could reach 9.4 ft MLLW for this 
evening's high tide in Fort Pulaski (approx. at 801PM), thus 
this will be close to yielding minor coastal flooding impacts 
across lower South Carolina and southeast Georgia. However, as 
it remains borderline, we will continue to monitor conditions 
through the next several hours and will issue a Coastal Flood 
Advisory if it seems warranted. Additionally, guidance indicates
tomorrow morning's and Sunday morning's high tide could also 
see minor coastal flooding.
